6                    WESTERN DISTRICT OF WASHINGTON                           
                               AT SEATTLE

     STEVEN FLOYD, et al.,           CASE NO. C22-1599-KKE                    
8                                                                             

                   Plaintiff(s),     ORDER ON DEFENDANTS’ MOTION TO           
9                                                                             
          v.                         COMPEL                                   

10                                                                             
     AMAZON.COM INC., et al.,                                                 

11                                                                             
                    Defendant(s).                                             

12                                                                             
         Defendants Amazon.com Inc. and Apple Inc. filed a motion to compel production of 11 
13                                                                             
    communications between Plaintiff Steven Floyd and his attorneys, arguing that by affirmatively 
14                                                                             
    putting the content of those communications “at issue” in this case, Floyd implicitly waived any 
15                                                                             
    privilege that protected those communications.  Dkt. No. 172 at 10–11.1  The Court has considered 
16                                                                             
    the parties’ briefing and heard oral argument on the motion.  See Dkt. No. 187.  Because 
17                                                                             
    Defendants have failed to show that the communications are “at issue” with respect to any claim 
18                                                                             
    or defense asserted in this litigation, the Court finds that the actions of Floyd and/or his counsel 
19                                                                             
    do not constitute an implied waiver.                                      
20                                                                             
         Thus, the Court will deny Defendants’ motion to compel but, as explained herein, may 
21                                                                             
    nonetheless order Plaintiffs to submit some of Floyd’s communications for in camera review for 
22                                                                             
23                                                                             

24   1 This order refers to the parties’ briefing using CM/ECF page numbers.   
1   purposes of resolving Plaintiffs’ counsel’s motion to withdraw and Defendants’ motion for 
2   discovery sanctions, if those motions are reactivated.                    
3                           I.   BACKGROUND                                   

4        On February 29, 2024, Floyd filed a motion for leave to amend the complaint to add new 
5   plaintiffs, based on counsel’s representation that although Floyd had not expressed an intent to 
6   withdraw as a named Plaintiff, he had, since January 16, become “difficult to reach” and could be 
7   experiencing “some type of personal emergency.”  Dkt. No. 80 at 8.  Plaintiffs’ counsel began a 
8   search for additional plaintiffs on January 24, and ultimately found two class members willing to 
9   serve as class representatives.  Id.                                      
10        The Court granted Floyd’s motion for leave, acknowledging the authority permitting 
11   amendment where a class representative ceases communicating or seeks to withdraw.  See Dkt. 
12   No. 98.  The Court’s order assumed that, based on counsel’s representations, Floyd would be 

13   continuing in the litigation and that, for example, his adequacy as a named plaintiff would be 
14   adjudicated at a future point.  See id. at 4–5.  Because counsel represented that Floyd had not 
15   withdrawn and intended to stay part of the class, the Court found that the motion to amend did not 
16   constitute a back-door attempt to begin the action anew.  Id.             
17        After the Court granted Plaintiffs’ motion to amend, Defendants immediately renewed their 
18   efforts to depose Floyd and seek other forms of discovery from him.  See Dkt. No. 104.  Those 
19   efforts  proved  unsuccessful  because  Floyd  was  not  communicating  with  his  attorneys,  and 
20   Defendants moved to compel responses to outstanding discovery requests.  Id.  In response to the 
21   motion to compel, Floyd’s attorneys filed a cross-motion to withdraw him as a class representative, 
22   but indicated that he was not dismissing his claims with prejudice and that he wished to remain 

23   part of the proposed class.  See Dkt. No. 114 at 17.                      
24                                                                             
1        In light of the fact that Floyd retained his status as a class representative even after the 
2   complaint was amended, and based on a finding that Defendants would be prejudiced without the 
3   discovery they seek from Floyd, the Court granted Defendants’ motion to compel discovery and 

4   indicated that Floyd’s cross-motion to withdraw as a class representative would not be adjudicated 
5   until after he complied with the order compelling discovery.  Dkt. No. 132.  That order was entered 
6   on August 16, 2024, and required that Floyd respond to discovery requests by August 30, 2024, 
7   and to sit for deposition by September 30, 2024.  Id. at 8.               
8        On August 29, Plaintiffs filed a stipulated motion asking for an extension of the August 30 
9   deadline to September 13, indicating that counsel had been able to reestablish communication with 
10   Floyd and were hopeful that he could comply with his discovery obligations with a modest 
11   extension.  Dkt. No. 134.  Counsel represented that the parties did not anticipate an extension of 
12   the deposition deadline.  Id. ¶ 6.  Defendants agreed to that extension and the Court granted the 

13   stipulated motion the same day.  Dkt. Nos. 134, 135.                      
14        On September 13—the new deadline for Floyd’s discovery responses—Plaintiffs’ counsel 
15   filed a motion to withdraw, saying that their relationship with Floyd fundamentally broke down 
16                                                                             
    since their last communication with him on August 28.  Dkt. No. 140 at 4–5.  Apple2 opposed the 
17   motion to withdraw, on the grounds that withdrawal should be conditioned upon an extension of 
18   Floyd’s  discovery  deadlines,  and  Plaintiffs’  counsel’s  production  of  all  of  their  2024 
19   communications with Floyd to the Court for in camera review to determine the degree to which 
20   any of counsel’s statements/filings during that time had been authorized by Floyd himself.  Dkt. 
21   No. 143.  Defendants also filed their own motion for discovery sanctions against Floyd, which 
22   Floyd’s counsel did not oppose.  Dkt. Nos. 152, 156.                      
23                                                                             

    2 Amazon took no position on Floyd’s counsel’s motion to withdraw representation and did not join Apple’s 
24   opposition.  Dkt. No. 145.                                                
1        The Court denied the motion to withdraw and the motion for sanctions without prejudice, 
2   pending Plaintiffs’ counsel’s production of all non-privileged communications with Floyd in 2024, 
3   as well as a privilege log for the withheld communications, to flesh out the record “in order to 

4   resolve questions of delay, prejudice, and harm to the administration of justice.”  Dkt. No. 168.  
5   The Court indicated that those motions could be reactivated after any future motion related to the 
6   production of Floyd’s communications is resolved.  Id. at 3.              
7        Plaintiffs’ counsel complied with this order, and Defendants filed a motion to compel 11 
8   of the communications listed on the Plaintiffs’ privilege log.  Dkt. No. 172.  For the following 
9   reasons, the Court finds that because Defendants have not shown that the attorney-client privilege 
10   has been waived with respect to those communications, their motion to compel their production 
11   will be denied.                                                           
12                             II.  ANALYSIS                                   

13        The Ninth Circuit has described the attorney-client privilege in a multi-part explanation:  
14        (1) When legal advice of any kind is sought (2) from a professional legal adviser in 
         his or her capacity as such, (3) the communications relating to that purpose, 
15        (4) made  in  confidence  (5)  by  the  client,  (6)  are,  at  the  client’s  instance, 
         permanently protected (7) from disclosure by the client or by the legal adviser 
16        (8) unless the protection be waived.                                 

17   United States v. Martin, 278 F.3d 988, 999 (9th Cir. 2002).  “The burden is on the party asserting 
18   the privilege to establish all the elements of the privilege.”  Id. at 999–1000.   
19        The attorney-client privilege is implicitly waived “when the privilege holder raises a claim 
20   or defense that puts privileged communications at issue.”  Apple Inc. v. Samsung Elecs. Co., Ltd., 
21   306 F.R.D. 234, 241 (N.D. Cal. 2015).  Privileged communications are “at issue” when:  
22        (1) assertion of the privilege was the result of some affirmative act, such as filing 
         suit, by the asserting party; (2) through this affirmative act, the asserting party put 
23        the  protected  information  at  issue  by  making  it  relevant  to  the  case;  and 
         (3) application of the privilege would have denied the opposing party access to 
24        information vital to his defense.                                    
1                                                                             
    Hearn v. Rhay, 68 F.R.D. 574, 581 (E.D. Wash. 1975).  “Privileged communications do not 
2                                                                             
    become discoverable simply because they are related to issues raised in the litigation, [but] where 
3                                                                             
    a party raises a claim which in fairness requires disclosure of the protected communication, the 
4                                                                             
    privilege may be implicitly waived.”  Apple, 306 F.R.D. at 241 (cleaned up). 
5                                                                             
         Defendants  agree  with  Plaintiffs  that  Floyd’s  communications  with  his  counsel  are 
6                                                                             
    protected by the attorney-client privilege (Dkt. No. 192 at 23, 33), but contend that this privilege 
7                                                                             
    was waived by counsel’s affirmative acts in filing the motion for leave to amend the complaint.  
8                                                                             
    The Court disagrees.  While Floyd’s privileged communications are relevant to issues raised in 
9                                                                             
    litigation, the Court does not find that any of Floyd’s affirmative acts went so far as to raise a claim 
10                                                                             
    that “in fairness requires disclosure” of his protected communications to opposing counsel.  
11                                                                             
    Floyd’s communications (and lack thereof) were referenced generally in the motion for leave to 
12                                                                             
    amend the complaint, to explain why the motion was filed, but those communications and that 
13                                                                             
    motion were not directly connected to any claim in the amended complaint or any defense thereto.   
14                                                                             
         Without a connection to a claim or defense asserted in this case, the Court does not find 
15                                                                             
    that Floyd has taken an affirmative act that placed his communications “at issue” for purposes of 
16                                                                             
    the Hearn test.  See, e.g., United States v. Amlani, 169 F.3d 1189, 1195 (9th Cir. 1999) (where 
17                                                                             
    defendant appealed his criminal conviction based on a Sixth Amendment claim asserting that his 
18                                                                             
    attorney disparaged him, which led him to discharge that attorney and retain inexperienced counsel 
19                                                                             
    who provided inadequate representation: “[Defendant] cannot assert that certain factors caused 
20                                                                             
    him  to  discharge  his  attorney  and  then  invoke  the  attorney-client  privilege  to  prevent  the 
21                                                                             
    government from examining the situation further.”); 3D Sys., Inc. v. Wynne, No.: 21-cv-1141-
22                                                                             
    AGS-DDL, 2024 WL 940318, at *6 (S.D. Cal. Feb. 21, 2024) (finding that because the statute of 
23                                                                             
    limitations on plaintiff’s trade secret misappropriation claims “began running when it knew or had 
24                                                                             
1   reason to know of the injury that is the basis of the action and the cause of that injury,” the 
2   privileged information pertaining to plaintiff’s internal investigation would “go to the heart of 
3   whether it knew or had reason to know” of defendants’ alleged misappropriation and it was 

4   therefore “at issue” (cleaned up)); Sorensen v. Black & Decker Corp., No. 06cv1572-BTM (CAB), 
5   2007 WL 1976652, at *2 (S.D. Cal. Apr. 9, 2007) (“The privilege is waived only when a party 
6   chooses to utilize the [privileged] information to advance a claim or defense.”); Aloe Vera of Am., 
7   Inc. v. United States, No. CV 99-1794-PHX-JAT, 2003 WL 22429082, at *3 (D. Ariz. Sep. 23, 
8   2003) (finding that privileged documents were “at issue” for purposes of proving defendant’s 
9   statute of limitations defense).                                          
10        Here, Floyd’s privileged communications formed the factual backdrop for the motion for 
11   leave to amend (as well as the subsequent motion to withdraw as a class representative and 
12   counsel’s motion to withdraw representation), but the content of the communications did not 

13   establish any element of a claim or defense raised in the litigation.  Defendants suggest that if 
14   Floyd had instructed his counsel to dismiss his claims, this instruction would have (or should have) 
15   led to the dismissal of the action entirely, but this position is not supported by authority in and out 
16   of this circuit.  See, e.g., Vue v. Pentagon Fed. Credit Union, No. 1:21-cv-01063-JLT-SAB, 2024 
17   WL 4436814, at *3–7 (E.D. Cal. Oct. 4, 2024) (citing cases as support for granting a motion for 
18   leave to amend a complaint to substitute class representatives, over defendants’ objection that 
19   plaintiff did not authorize her attorneys to file the motion for leave to amend); see also Phillips v. 
20   Ford Motor Co., 435 F.3d 785, 787 (7th Cir. 2006) (“Strictly speaking, if no motion to certify has 
21   been filed … the case is not yet a class action and so a dismissal of the named plaintiffs’ claims 
22   should end the case.  If the case is later restarted with a new plaintiff, it is a new commencement, 

23   a new suit.  But the courts, both federal and Illinois, are not so strict.  Unless jurisdiction never 
24                                                                             
1   attached, or the attempt to substitute comes long after the claims of the named plaintiffs were 
2   dismissed, substitution for the named plaintiffs is allowed.” (cleaned up)).   
3        That the privileged communications may reveal ethical lapses by Floyd’s counsel is an 

4   insufficient basis on which to compel their production (see, e.g., Dkt. No. 192 at 22–29); this Court 
5   is not tasked with, as a general matter, policing attorney-client relationships nor monitoring 
6   counsel’s compliance with the Rules of Professional Responsibility.  Because the motion presently 
7   before the Court seeks production of Floyd’s communications to Defendants, and the Court finds 
8   that the protection afforded those communications has not been waived here, the Court will deny 
9   the motion.                                                               
10        But even if the Court will not grant Defendants’ motion to compel production of Floyd’s 
11   communications,  the  Court  nonetheless  finds  it  would  be  necessary  to  review  Floyd’s 
12   communications in camera for purposes of resolving two motions that have been terminated while 

13   the  Court  considered  whether  Floyd’s  communications  should  be  produced  to  Defendants: 
14   Plaintiffs’ counsel’s motion to withdraw representation and Defendants’ motion for discovery 
15   sanctions against Floyd.  See Dkt. Nos. 140, 152.  Given that Floyd himself has ceased participating 
16   in this litigation, the Court must turn to other sources for the information necessary to resolve these 
17   motions.  The record currently before the Court is inadequate to determine whether Plaintiffs’ 
18   counsel’s withdrawal of representation is appropriate with or without the conditions requested by 
19   Apple.  See Dkt. No. 143.  “The decision to grant or deny counsel’s motion to withdraw is 
20   ultimately committed to the discretion of the trial court[,]” and the Court requires more information 
21   about Floyd’s relationship with his counsel in order to exercise that discretion.  Fujifilm Sonosite, 
22   Inc. v. Imaging Specialists Grp., LLC, No. C13-983 RSM, 2014 WL 1400992, at *1 (W.D. Wash. 

23   Apr. 10, 2014).                                                           
24                                                                             
1        Likewise, the Court cannot resolve the motion for discovery sanctions against Floyd 
2   without understanding what he may have communicated to his counsel regarding his intentions 
3   with respect to discovery and/or pursuing his claims in this litigation.  Federal Rule of Civil 

4   Procedure 37(b)(2)(A) empowers the Court to enter “just orders” to address a party’s failure to 
5   obey a discovery order, and the Court cannot determine what is just in this scenario without more 
6   information that may be available upon review of Floyd’s communications.    
7                           III.  CONCLUSION                                  
8        For these reasons, the Court DENIES Defendants’ motion to compel.  Dkt. No. 172.   
9        The parties are directed to consider, in light of this ruling, whether to reactivate Plaintiffs’ 
10   counsel’s motion to withdraw as Floyd’s counsel (Dkt. No. 140) and/or Defendants’ motion for 
11   discovery sanctions (Dkt. No. 152).  Any party may file a notice of intent to reactivate no later 
12   than March 14, 2025.  If either motion is reactivated, the Court will provide further instruction on 

13   the in camera production required for the Court to adjudicate the motion(s). 
14        Dated this 7th day of March, 2025.                                   
15                                                                             
                                  A                                           
16                                                                             
                                  Kymberly K. Evanson                         
17                                 United States District Judge

21   been filed … the case is not yet a class action and so a dismissal of the named plaintiffs’ claims 
22   should end the case.  If the case is later restarted with a new plaintiff, it is a new commencement, 

23   a new suit.  But the courts, both federal and Illinois, are not so strict.  Unless jurisdiction never 
24                                                                             
1   attached, or the attempt to substitute comes long after the claims of the named plaintiffs were 
2   dismissed, substitution for the named plaintiffs is allowed.” (cleaned up)).   
3        That the privileged communications may reveal ethical lapses by Floyd’s counsel is an 

4   insufficient basis on which to compel their production (see, e.g., Dkt. No. 192 at 22–29); this Court 
5   is not tasked with, as a general matter, policing attorney-client relationships nor monitoring 
6   counsel’s compliance with the Rules of Professional Responsibility.  Because the motion presently 
7   before the Court seeks production of Floyd’s communications to Defendants, and the Court finds 
8   that the protection afforded those communications has not been waived here, the Court will deny 
9   the motion.                                                               
10        But even if the Court will not grant Defendants’ motion to compel production of Floyd’s 
11   communications,  the  Court  nonetheless  finds  it  would  be  necessary  to  review  Floyd’s 
12   communications in camera for purposes of resolving two motions that have been terminated while 

13   the  Court  considered  whether  Floyd’s  communications  should  be  produced  to  Defendants: 
14   Plaintiffs’ counsel’s motion to withdraw representation and Defendants’ motion for discovery 
15   sanctions against Floyd.  See Dkt. Nos. 140, 152.  Given that Floyd himself has ceased participating 
16   in this litigation, the Court must turn to other sources for the information necessary to resolve these 
17   motions.  The record currently before the Court is inadequate to determine whether Plaintiffs’ 
18   counsel’s withdrawal of representation is appropriate with or without the conditions requested by 
19   Apple.  See Dkt. No. 143.  “The decision to grant or deny counsel’s motion to withdraw is 
20   ultimately committed to the discretion of the trial court[,]” and the Court requires more information 
21   about Floyd’s relationship with his counsel in order to exercise that discretion.  Fujifilm Sonosite, 
22   Inc. v. Imaging Specialists Grp., LLC, No. C13-983 RSM,
2014 WL 1400992
, at *1 (W.D. Wash. 

23   Apr. 10, 2014).

1        Likewise, the Court cannot resolve the motion for discovery sanctions against Floyd 
2   without understanding what he may have communicated to his counsel regarding his intentions 
3   with respect to discovery and/or pursuing his claims in this litigation.  Federal Rule of Civil 

4   Procedure 37(b)(2)(A) empowers the Court to enter “just orders” to address a party’s failure to 
5   obey a discovery order, and the Court cannot determine what is just in this scenario without more 
6   information that may be available upon review of Floyd’s communications.    
7                           III.  CONCLUSION                                  
8        For these reasons, the Court DENIES Defendants’ motion to compel.  Dkt. No. 172.   
9        The parties are directed to consider, in light of this ruling, whether to reactivate Plaintiffs’ 
10   counsel’s motion to withdraw as Floyd’s counsel (Dkt. No. 140) and/or Defendants’ motion for 
11   discovery sanctions (Dkt. No. 152).  Any party may file a notice of intent to reactivate no later 
12   than March 14, 2025.  If either motion is reactivated, the Court will provide further instruction on 

13   the in camera production required for the Court to adjudicate the motion(s).
